Keep your eye on the ball and you'll be fine.
forms: keep our eye on the ball
take your eye off the ball

gloss: Learn how to do a job or activity.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: It took me a few weeks to learn the ropes.
Jane will show you the ropes.

gloss: Release pent-up energy or emotion.
usage: Common British phrase; Americans also say 'blow off steam'.
examples: The kids need to let off steam after school.
I go running to let off steam.

gloss: Relax and enjoy yourself freely.
usage: Common in British and American English.
pragmatic_note: At a work party, letting your hair down is fine, but not too much.
examples: The office party is a chance to let your hair down.
It's good to let your hair down sometimes.

headword: the life and soul of the party
gloss: Someone lively who makes social events fun.
usage: Distinctively British phrase.
examples: Gran was always the life and soul of the party.
He's the life and soul of any party.
forms: life and soul of the party

gloss: Rather old, often too old for something.
usage: Common British phrase, often self-deprecating.
pragmatic_note: Safest about yourself or things; about others it can sound ageist.
examples: I'm getting a bit long in the tooth for festivals.
The software's looking long in the tooth.

headword: make hay while the sun shines
gloss: Take advantage of good conditions while they last.
usage: Common British proverb.
examples: Sales are strong, so let's make hay while the sun shines.
Make hay while the sun shines, I say.

gloss: I will keep it secret.
usage: Common British phrase; 'mum' here means silent.
pitfall: Nothing to do with mothers; 'mum' means saying nothing.
examples: Don't worry, mum's the word.
It's a surprise party, so mum's the word.

headword: nail your colours to the mast
gloss: Declare your position or support openly and firmly.
usage: Distinctively British phrase, common in politics.
examples: The minister has nailed her colours to the mast on this.
It's time to nail our colours to the mast.
forms: nailed his colours to the mast

headword: a nod's as good as a wink
gloss: A hint is enough; no need to say more.
usage: British phrase, often implying knowing complicity.
pragmatic_note: Associated with comic innuendo; casual use only.
examples: Say no more: a nod's as good as a wink.
He knew what I meant; a nod's as good as a wink.
forms: a nod is as good as a wink

gloss: Old-fashioned or no longer interesting.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: Video calls are old hat now.
That idea's a bit old hat.

gloss: With very little money.
usage: Neutral and common.
examples: We started the business on a shoestring.
They made the film on a shoestring budget.

gloss: In a state of nervous suspense.
usage: Common British phrase.
examples: We were on tenterhooks waiting for the results.
Don't keep me on tenterhooks!

gloss: Catch someone unprepared.
usage: Distinctively British phrase.
examples: The question caught me on the hop.
The early deadline caught us all on the hop.

gloss: Recovering from illness or injury.
usage: Common British phrase.
examples: He's been ill, but he's on the mend now.
My knee's on the mend, thanks.

gloss: In serious difficulty and likely to fail, especially a relationship.
usage: Common in British and American English; also means a drink served with ice.
examples: Their marriage is on the rocks.
The company's finances are on the rocks.

gloss: In a risky situation where a mistake could cause trouble.
usage: Common in British and American English, often 'skating on thin ice'.
examples: You're on thin ice after being late twice.
The government is skating on thin ice.

gloss: A bad experience makes you more cautious.
usage: Common British proverb.
examples: I'm not lending him money again: once bitten, twice shy.
Once bitten, twice shy, as they say.

gloss: Behaviour that is unacceptable or unfair.
usage: Informal British use, often 'well out of order'.
pitfall: It also means 'not working' on signs, e.g. a broken lift.
examples: What he said to you was out of order.
That's well out of order, mate.

gloss: In an isolated or risky position, without support.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: I went out on a limb to recommend him.
She's out on a limb with that view.

gloss: In a position where you have no choice.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: The supplier has us over a barrel.
They had him over a barrel.

gloss: What you would normally expect.
usage: Common in British and American English, from golf.
pragmatic_note: Often used with weary resignation.
examples: Delays are par for the course on this line.
Long hours are par for the course in law.

gloss: Argue the opposite view to test an argument.
usage: Neutral and common in meetings and debates.
pragmatic_note: Announcing it first is polite: it signals you are not attacking the idea personally.
examples: Let me play devil's advocate for a moment.
She often plays devil's advocate.

gloss: Behave in a way intended to win popular approval.
usage: British phrase common in politics.
examples: The minister was clearly playing to the gallery.
Stop playing to the gallery and answer the question.

gloss: Die.
usage: Jokey British euphemism, mainly northern.
pragmatic_note: Comic; never use about a real bereavement.
examples: I want to travel before I pop my clogs.
When I pop my clogs, you can have the house.

headword: the pot calling the kettle black
gloss: Criticising someone for a fault you also have.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: He called me lazy? That's the pot calling the kettle black.
Talk about the pot calling the kettle black.

gloss: Calm a tense or angry situation.
usage: Neutral and common.
examples: She tried to pour oil on troubled waters after the row.
The chair poured oil on troubled waters.

gloss: Relax and rest.
usage: Common British phrase.
examples: I'm going to put my feet up with a cup of tea.
You deserve to put your feet up.

headword: put your money where your mouth is
gloss: Back up your words with action or money.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: If you believe in it, put your money where your mouth is.
It's time the council put its money where its mouth is.

gloss: Think very hard to remember or solve something.
usage: Common British phrase.
examples: I've been racking my brains trying to remember her name.
Rack your brains: when did you last see it?

gloss: Decline an invitation now, suggesting another time.
usage: American in origin (baseball) but widely used in the UK.
pitfall: US-leaning; it works in the UK but sounds slightly American.
examples: Can I take a rain check on lunch?
I'll take a rain check, if that's all right.

gloss: Basic and unpolished but adequate.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: It's a rough and ready estimate.
The campsite was a bit rough and ready.

gloss: Be in charge; be the dominant person.
usage: Common British phrase.
examples: In our house the cat rules the roost.
She rules the roost in that department.

gloss: A good, honest, decent person.
usage: Common British phrase, often of ordinary hard-working people.
pragmatic_note: Warm praise, with a hint of class: often said of working-class people.
examples: Her parents are the salt of the earth.
He's salt of the earth, always helping out.

gloss: Rescue someone from trouble.
usage: Informal British phrase.
examples: Thanks for covering for me; you saved my bacon.
The backup saved our bacon.

gloss: Something you do so often it happens automatically.
usage: Neutral and common.
examples: After a while, driving on the left becomes second nature.
Checking my email is second nature.

gloss: Become suddenly very angry.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: I saw red when he insulted my mum.
She sees red if anyone is rude to waiters.

gloss: Damage your own interests through foolishness.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: Cutting the training budget is shooting yourself in the foot.
He really shot himself in the foot there.

headword: six of one and half a dozen of the other
gloss: There is little difference between the two options.
usage: Common British phrase.
examples: Train or coach? It's six of one and half a dozen of the other.
Who started it? Six of one, half a dozen of the other.
forms: six of one, half a dozen of the other

gloss: Sleep very deeply.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: I slept like a log after the walk.
You'll sleep like a log tonight.

gloss: Something unimportant or of little value.
usage: Distinctively British phrase.
examples: Compared with the main contract, this is small beer.
Ten thousand pounds is small beer to them.

gloss: Deception designed to mislead or obscure the truth.
usage: Common in British and American English, often about statistics or politics.
examples: The so-called savings are just smoke and mirrors.
It's all smoke and mirrors.

gloss: Argue over tiny, unimportant differences.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: Let's not split hairs over the wording.
You're splitting hairs now.

gloss: A tense, nerve-racking final stage of a competition.
usage: Informal British football phrase, popularised by Sir Alex Ferguson.
pragmatic_note: Comic and slightly cheeky; colleagues may enjoy it, clients may not.
examples: It's squeaky bum time in the title race.
Two weeks to the deadline: squeaky bum time.

gloss: Refuse to back down or change position.
usage: Neutral and common.
examples: She stood her ground in the negotiation.
Stand your ground if you're sure.

gloss: Interfere by giving an unwanted opinion.
usage: Informal British phrase.
examples: Nobody asked him to stick his oar in.
Sorry to stick my oar in, but that's wrong.

gloss: Decide to do something bold or risky.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: We've finally taken the plunge and bought a house.
Take the plunge and apply.

gloss: Deal calmly with something difficult.
usage: British phrase; Americans say 'in stride'.
examples: She took the redundancy in her stride.
He takes everything in his stride.

gloss: A decision or opinion has not yet been reached.
usage: Neutral and common.
examples: The jury's still out on the new system.
The jury is still out on whether it works.

gloss: The largest part of something.
usage: Neutral and common.
examples: London gets the lion's share of the funding.
She did the lion's share of the work.

gloss: The people in authority, often unnamed.
usage: Common in British and American English, slightly ironic.
pragmatic_note: Slightly ironic way to refer to senior management.
examples: The powers that be have decided to close the canteen.
We're waiting for the powers that be to approve it.

gloss: The genuine article, not an imitation.
usage: Slightly dated British and American phrase.
examples: This Scotch is the real McCoy.
Is that painting the real McCoy?

headword: the writing is on the wall
gloss: There are clear signs of coming failure or disaster.
usage: Neutral and common in British English.
examples: The writing was on the wall for the high-street chain.
Once sales fell, the writing was on the wall.
forms: the writing was on the wall

gloss: Scarce; few in number.
usage: Distinctively British phrase.
examples: Volunteers are thin on the ground this year.
Good ideas were thin on the ground.

gloss: Act recklessly without worrying about risks.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: We threw caution to the wind and booked first class.
Sometimes you have to throw caution to the wind.

gloss: Spend less money than before.
usage: Common in British news and conversation.
examples: Families are having to tighten their belts.
We'll all need to tighten our belts this year.

gloss: For a very long time, possibly forever.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: You can argue till the cows come home, but I won't change.
We could talk till the cows come home.

gloss: As well; in addition.
usage: Common in British and American English, added at the end of a sentence.
examples: The flat is cheap, and close to the station to boot.
She's clever, and funny to boot.

gloss: Of the highest quality or social class.
usage: British phrase.
examples: That was a top-drawer performance.
The guests were all top drawer.

gloss: Offend someone by getting involved in their area of responsibility.
usage: British phrase; Americans say 'step on someone's toes'.
pragmatic_note: 'I don't want to tread on anyone's toes' is a polite way to offer help.
examples: I don't want to tread on anyone's toes.
Be careful not to tread on the finance team's toes.

gloss: Start behaving in a better way.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: After the warning, he turned over a new leaf.
I'm turning over a new leaf this year.

gloss: Reverse a situation to gain the advantage.
usage: Neutral and common.
examples: The underdogs turned the tables in the second half.
She turned the tables on her critics.

gloss: Kept secret.
usage: Neutral and common.
examples: The new design is being kept under wraps.
Details remain under wraps until Monday.

gloss: Available for anyone to obtain.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: Three prizes are up for grabs.
The top job is up for grabs.

gloss: Survive a difficult period.
usage: Neutral and common.
examples: The company weathered the storm of the recession.
We'll weather the storm.

gloss: Completely; thoroughly.
usage: Common British intensifier.
examples: We were well and truly lost.
The summer is well and truly over.

gloss: When a situation becomes critical and action is needed.
usage: Common in British and American English.
examples: When push comes to shove, she'll support us.
When push comes to shove, safety comes first.
